newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Alabian port springs to life as troops land.
newsitem.headline: Alabian port springs to life as troops land.

text.p: On the seafront just beyond the gates of Albania's main port is a huge Stalinist era statue of a soldier with his rifle aloft, looking out to sea.
His gaze seemed to focuson a flotilla of grey warships on the horizon as "D-Day" dawned on Tuesday and a multinational security force for the troubled Balkan state began to deploy.
First to land were 450 French troops whose ship docked in the dilapidated port of Durres at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT), an hour after the end of Albania's dusk-to-dawn curfew.
The port, 40 km (25 miles) west of the capital Tirana, stood idle last month when chaos spread across Albania and only recently reopened.
"It's pretty impressive," said Pjeter Jame, a teacher from Tirana who made a special trip to Durres to watch the landing of the Italian-led force. Its job will be to secure aid convoys.
Beggars, a common sight on the streets of Europe's poorest country, were more interested in the pack of reporters.
While French troops unloaded their tanks and trucks, an Italian amphibious assault ship moored alongside and paratroopers in red berets marched off.
Several hours later, the first of 350 Spanish troops disembarked from two ships and gathered on the docks, their rucksacks heaped besides them, looking a little forlorn as they awaited orders.
Outside the gates of Durres port, the start of the long-awaited "Operation Alba" drew a small crowd. The mission's name means "dawn" in Italian.

A couple of bystanders leaned against bicycles observing the bustle as Albanian police waved cars to a halt to let a troop convoy pass. One elderly man who served in the Albanian navy for 25 years put on his old black uniform for the occasion.
"They can stay as long as they like," said Ali Velci as he headed for a commercial ferry bound for Italy, where he has a job. "I'm very happy. Albania needs a lot of help."
On the quayside next to the ship, where Italy's 200 troops were unloading, a private consignment of sacks of flour was being winched into trucks from a rusting Albanian ship.
"There's nothing for all these soldiers to do," said one lorry driver who declined to be named. "Maybe it would have been better to send them to the south."

Apart from the armed police check-points at the entry to Durres, city life seemed normal. But bullet holes in the window of a deserted shop were a reminder of the mayhem that swept the country at the end of February after the collapse of dubious savings schemes with the life savings of countless Albanians.

The security mission has no mandate to repossess rifles looted from army depots at the height of the insurrection and southern Albania, still largely in the hands of anti-government rebels, remains potentially risky bandit country.

Frederic, a French solider just back from Sarajevo, said he was not looking for action in Albania. He was more worried about where he could buy a radio. The camp the French will stay in outside Durres is in bad shape with no water or electricity.
"I think we're going to get bored," he said.
